passage: "How will you sort all of these?" asked Kishore, raising his eyebrows at the heap. "Easy," said Rukmini. "If it has wheels, it goes in the blue box." She held up a red car. "Wheels. Blue box." Then a truck. "Wheels. Blue box." "And the scooter?" "Has wheels," she said, and dropped it in with a clunk. "See, Bhaiya? I don't have to ask you every time." Kishore grinned. "Then I'll do the books."

qa.q: Which box did the wheeled toys go into?
qa.a: The car, the truck and the scooter all went into the blue box.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling about her rule when she said she did not have to ask every time?
qa.a: Rukmini felt proud and sure of herself. Her quick answers and the clunk of the scooter show she trusts her rule.

qa.q: What other approach could work for the rest of the mess, and why?
qa.a: Rukmini could make a second rule, like "If it has pages, it goes on the shelf." A rule lets her sort without stopping to ask.

qa.q: How does Kishore see Rukmini's rule?
qa.a: Kishore sees that it works, so he grins and takes the books himself. He is glad not to be asked about every toy.

grounding: A child sorts toys by an if-then rule about wheels and needs no help with each item.

passage:
Kindergarten note for Chandrika's parents
At clean-up time Chandrika made up a rule: "If it has wheels, it goes in the blue box." She sorted three cars, a dump truck and a toy scooter without asking me once. Parveen tried to put a doll in the blue box, and Chandrika said, "No wheels!" I praised her rule and suggested another for the red box.

qa.q: Where did the wheeled toys go?
What was Chandrika thinking when she said "No wheels!"?
qa.a: She felt sure and confident in her rule, keeping the blue box for wheels only.

qa.q: What else could Chandrika add to her rule?
qa.a: A second rule, like "soft things go in the red box," so every toy has a place.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel being corrected?
qa.a: Parveen might feel a bit embarrassed, or curious about the rule.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child sorting toys by the rule "if it has wheels, it goes in the blue box" without asking each time.

passage: In the small house near the Ranchi bus stand, Parveen tidied up. Her aunt Indu had said, "If it has wheels, it goes in the blue box." Parveen picked up a car: wheels. Blue box. A truck: wheels. Blue box. A doll: no wheels. She put it on the bed. A scooter: she spun its wheel. Blue box. She sorted the rest without asking once.

qa.q: Who had given Parveen the rule?
qa.a: Her aunt Indu had said it.

qa.q: What was Parveen thinking when she spun the scooter's wheel?
qa.a: She was checking her rule, feeling confident and proud of getting it right.

qa.q: What would you advise Indu to add next?
qa.a: Another rule for the dolls and soft toys, so Parveen can sort everything herself.

qa.q: How might Indu see Parveen's sorting?
qa.a: Indu would likely feel pleased that the rule works and Parveen doesn't need to ask.

grounding: A child sorts toys using the rule that anything with wheels goes in the blue box.
